opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to where the real demand and the real data were at that moment.

When we started, embodied intelligence was an exciting idea, but the commercial reality was thin. Humanoid robots and general-purpose manipulation were mostly demos. There wasn't yet a large customer base willing to pay steadily for the infrastructure behind them. Autonomous driving was different. It was the one domain where a physical AI system was already deployed at scale, generating huge amounts of real-world data, and where companies were spending serious money on data collection, annotation, simulation, training pipelines, and evaluation.

So we asked ourselves: what does embodied intelligence fundamentally need? It needs a perception-to-action loop working in the messy physical world. It needs multimodal sensor data, camera, lidar, and so on, handled at enormous volume. It needs ways to find long-tail corner cases, to simulate and reconstruct scenes, and to close the loop between data and model iteration. Autonomous driving had all of those problems, earlier and more intensely than anyone else. In a sense, a car is the first embodied agent that's actually been commercialized at scale. It just happens to have wheels instead of arms.

Serving driving first let us do a few things at once. First, we could survive and grow, because there were paying customers with urgent needs, and in a startup that matters a lot. Second, we built our toolchain and data engine against the hardest real-world standards. Driving customers are extremely demanding about safety, about coverage of rare scenarios, and about data quality, so that pressure made our infrastructure much more robust. Third, a lot of what we learned transfers directly: 4D spatial understanding, scene reconstruction, automated labeling, world-model-style simulation, data flywheels. When robotics companies began to need the same capabilities, we weren't starting from zero. We were extending something already battle-tested.

There's also a timing argument. Technology waves in physical AI tend to move from more structured to less structured environments. Roads are complex, but they're still relatively structured, with rules, lanes and signs. Homes, factories and general manipulation are much more open-ended. Riding the driving wave let us build our capabilities on the more tractable problem first, so we'd be ready when the less structured problems became commercially viable.

So I never saw autonomous driving as a detour. I saw it as the first chapter of embodied intelligence, the place where the industry's infrastructure was being forged. Our bet was that if we did that chapter really well, we'd naturally be positioned for the next one.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous driving was deployed at scale and generated huge amounts of real-world data, while describing the need to handle large volumes and cover rare scenarios.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that we sat down and decided embodied intelligence was the destination and then worked backwards. It was more that autonomous driving happened to be the one place where everything we cared about was already real.

Think about what embodied intelligence actually needs. You need a machine that perceives the physical world, makes decisions under uncertainty, and then acts on those decisions in a way that has real consequences. A car is exactly that. It has cameras, lidar, radar. It has to understand what a pedestrian is about to do. And if it gets the decision wrong, somebody gets hurt. So the engineering standards, the data standards, the safety culture, all of that is forced to a very high level, because nobody will tolerate anything less.

And the second thing, which I think people underestimate, is that autonomous driving had paying customers early. Robots in general did not. If you were building a humanoid in 2019, you were basically living on investor money and demo videos. If you were building sensing or compute or data infrastructure for autonomous vehicles, there were companies with budgets who needed the thing to work next quarter. That discipline matters enormously. It teaches you what reliability actually means, what deployment actually means, how to handle a fleet of thousands of machines instead of a lab prototype.

So our view was, if we go through that fire first, we come out with capabilities that transfer. The perception stack, the way you build a data closed loop, the way you handle edge cases at scale, the way you think about redundancy and failure. None of that is specific to cars. A car is just a robot with a very constrained task and a very large market.

And there was one more point. The car industry was already an industry. There was a supply chain, there were manufacturers, there were regulators. When you serve that, you learn how to work inside a mature industrial system, rather than inventing everything yourself. I believed, and I still believe, that embodied intelligence will eventually become an industry like that, and the companies that already know how to operate inside one will have a real advantage when it does.

r001.rationale: The response mentions data standards, data closed loops, and operating fleets at scale, but does not identify a need for more data in mass-produced autonomous-driving systems.

astra-6.text:
The way I saw it, autonomous driving was a concrete starting point for embodied intelligence. A vehicle has to perceive its surroundings, predict what might happen, make a decision, and act in the physical world. That whole loop is central to embodied intelligence.

It also had a clear commercial need. Teams needed ways to collect data, test systems, and improve reliability. Serving those needs offered a way to build useful capabilities while learning from real deployments.

Of course, you can’t simply take a driving system and put it into a robot. But the experience of connecting data, models, and physical actions—and making that loop work reliably—provides a foundation for moving into other embodied applications.

r001.rationale: The response says teams needed ways to collect data, but does not identify a need for more data in mass-produced autonomous-driving systems.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, our thinking was that autonomous driving was one of the clearest entry points into embodied intelligence. A vehicle has to perceive its surroundings, predict what might happen, make decisions, and act in the physical world. That brings many of the core challenges together in one application.

It also had a relatively clear commercial need. Developing and testing autonomous systems requires a lot of data and engineering support, so serving those teams offered a practical way to create value while learning what real-world deployment demands.

We didn’t assume that solving autonomous driving would automatically solve robotics. But we saw an opportunity to build capabilities around data, simulation, evaluation, and deployment that could eventually support a broader range of embodied systems.

r001.rationale: The response says developing and testing autonomous systems requires a lot of data, but it does not identify a data need specific to mass-produced autonomous-driving systems.
